extracted.intended_audience: conference program chairs, area chairs, reviewers, researchers interested in peer review processes and empirical studies of review consistency
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis and experimental protocol for measuring decision consistency in a large conference peer-review process (NeurIPS 2021), including metrics for disagreement, experimental design for duplicated reviews, limitations, and interpretation guidance for program chairs and reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duplicated-papers experimental design
rubrics_metrics.description: During assignment, choose 10% of papers uniformly at random as 'duplicated papers'. Create a copy of each duplicated paper and split ACs and reviewers at random between the two copies; assign two ACs and twice the normal number of reviewers to these papers. Ensure the two ACs are assigned to two different SACs so no SAC handled both copies. Any newly invited reviewer for one copy was automatically added as a conflict for the other copy. Committees were not told about the experiment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This procedural design is intended to create two independently reviewing committees for the same submissions while avoiding overlap of higher-level handlers (SACs) and reviewer conflicts. The design choice ensures independence of committees as much as possible while preserving normal review workflows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptance rule for duplicated papers
rubrics_metrics.description: Duplicated papers were accepted if at least one of the two copies was recommended for acceptance and no 'fatal flaw' was found.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This acceptance-by-one-committee rule resulted in some papers being accepted that would not have been without the experiment (92 accepted papers would not have been accepted otherwise). There were edge cases where one committee accepted but a 'fatal flaw' identified later led to rejection, and cases where committees disagreed about whether a flaw was fatal and the committees jointly determined conditions for conditional acceptance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fraction of inconsistent outcomes (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: The fraction of duplicated papers that were accepted by only one of the two committees (as either a poster, a spotlight, or an oral).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In 2021, 203 out of 882 duplicated papers were inconsistent, i.e., 23.0%. This is a basic, raw measure of decision inconsistency between independent committees reviewing the same paper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Random-baseline comparison for inconsistency
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare observed inconsistency to the expected inconsistency if each committee made acceptance decisions at random with probability equal to the observed acceptance rate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For duplicated papers the observed random-baseline expectation (with p=0.227) is 35.1% inconsistent outcomes. The observed 23.0% is closer to the random baseline than to 0, and the blog plots a gray curve showing expected inconsistent fractions across different acceptance rates to visualize the impact of changing selectivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjusted inconsistency treating 'bump' annotations as non-inconsistent
rubrics_metrics.description: If we do not consider pairs like 'Accept that can be bumped down' vs 'Reject', and 'Reject that can be bumped up' vs 'Poster Accept that shouldn’t be bumped up to Spotlight' as inconsistent, the fraction of inconsistent outcomes drops.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using this adjustment reduces the inconsistency fraction to 16%, reflecting that some disagreements reflect degree-of-confidence annotations (can be bumped up/down) rather than hard disagreement about accept/reject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept precision / arbitrariness
rubrics_metrics.description: Fraction of accepted papers that would have changed (been rejected) if the paper were re-reviewed; equivalent to 1 - accept_precision and related to 'arbitrariness' in earlier literature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In 2021, 50.6% of papers accepted by the first committee were rejected by the second (accept-precision complement). The probability that a randomly chosen rejected paper would have been accepted if re-reviewed was 14.9% (compared to 17.5% in 2014). These metrics quantify how many decisions are unstable on re-review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disagreement on orals/spotlights selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure of committee disagreement specifically for selection of orals and spotlights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There was especially high disagreement on which papers should be selected for orals and spotlights: more than half of all spotlights recommended by either committee were rejected by the other (examples: 13/25 and 13/23). This highlights that top-tier selection is highly variable between committees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Withdrawal rate after initial reviews
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare withdrawal rates after initial reviews between duplicated and non-duplicated papers as an indicator of authors' strategic behavior and second-shot effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors were most likely to withdraw if both copies were headed for rejection. The withdrawal rate after seeing initial reviews was 45% higher for papers not in the experiment compared with duplicated papers, suggesting duplicated papers' having two shots at acceptance reduces withdrawals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Categories of causes for disagreement (AC/SAC feedback)
rubrics_metrics.description: Based on AC and SAC surveys, disagreements tended to fall into three broad categories: (1) 'noise on the decision frontier' (borderline papers that could have gone either way), (2) genuine disagreements about value or severity of limitations (including intra-committee disagreement), and (3) cases where one committee found a significant issue the other did not (e.g., close prior work, incorrect proofs, methodological flaws).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Survey responses: 48% characterized cases as borderline/no real disagreement, 45% 'I still stand by our committee's decision', and 7% 'I believe the other committee made the right decision'. Feedback was limited (responses for 99 of 203 disagreeing papers and both committees' feedback for only 18 papers), which constrains analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authors' response-behavior as a confounder
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors of duplicated papers were asked to respond to each set of reviews independently, but some authors reported putting more effort into the copy they felt more likely to be accepted; in 50 pairs, authors only left comments on the copy with the higher average score.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This change in author behavior may skew experiment results: acceptance rate for non-duplicated papers was 25.8% vs duplicated papers' average acceptance rate of 22.7%, and non-overlapping 95% binomial CIs suggest authors changing behavior could account for differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Calibration edits and inconsistent meta-review fields as a limitation
rubrics_metrics.description: When decisions shifted during calibration, ACs were often asked to edit meta-reviews (e.g., moving poster ↔ reject or spotlight ↔ poster) but sometimes did not update the 'can be bumped up/down' fields, creating nonsensical combinations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples included 'reject' with 'can be bumped down'. Such inconsistencies in meta-review fields can introduce minor inaccuracies into analyses that rely on those fields to interpret disagreement or uncertainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact of shifting acceptance threshold
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyze how the fraction of inconsistent outcomes changes if the acceptance threshold is altered (e.g., accept only orals/spotlights, bump down/up rules applied).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: accepting only orals/spotlights yielded committees accepting 29 and 25 papers respectively but agreeing on only 3; bumping down posters marked as candidates reduces inconsistency by ~25% relative to random baseline; decisions made by NeurIPS 2021 ACs amount to ~35% relative improvement over random baseline. Visualizing these shifts helps understand tradeoffs between selectivity and arbitrariness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of AC certainty annotations ('sure' vs 'can be bumped')
rubrics_metrics.description: ACs were asked when entering recommendations to note whether they were sure or whether the paper could be bumped up or down; these annotations can be used to decide whether two differing recommendations constitute true inconsistency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treating 'can be bumped' annotations as indicating non-definitive recommendations reduces measured inconsistency (e.g., the 23.0% raw inconsistency reduced to 16% when such cases are considered not inconsistent). This shows value in recording meta-level confidence for interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation guidance for program chairs (selectivity vs arbitrariness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Key takeaway guidance: being significantly more selective will significantly increase arbitrariness (fraction of accepted papers that would have a different decision upon rereview), while increasing the acceptance rate may not appreciably decrease arbitrariness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Program chairs should weigh selectivity tradeoffs; the experiment shows no evidence that decision noise changed with scale since 2014. Also advise authors not to be overly discouraged by rejections since variability may reflect the review process rather than paper quality.
